stem.text: Which statement about an indifference curve is correct?

options.text: it always has a positive gradient
it can intersect with other indifference curves
its gradient is determined by the marginal rate of substitution
the higher the indifference curve the lower the utility gained

explanation.text: An indifference curve plots combinations of two goods giving a consumer equal utility. Its slope at any point is the marginal rate of substitution (MRS) — the rate at which the consumer would trade one good for the other while staying on the same utility level.

optionAnalysis.text: Indifference curves are normally downward sloping (negative gradient): to keep utility constant, more of one good must be offset by less of the other.
Indifference curves from the same consumer's preference map cannot intersect — two curves crossing would imply the same combination of goods gives two different utility levels, a contradiction.
The gradient of an indifference curve at any point is, by definition, the marginal rate of substitution between the two goods.
A higher indifference curve represents a higher level of utility, not lower — curves further from the origin are preferred.

reasoningChain: Recall that an indifference curve maps combinations of two goods giving equal utility.
Its slope at any point is defined as the marginal rate of substitution between the goods.
Check each statement against the standard properties: downward sloping, non-intersecting, higher curves = higher utility.

inferredMistakes.text: Confusing the direction of utility with distance from the origin, assuming curves further out somehow represent diminishing returns rather than greater total utility.
